summaries.example: Imagine two locked boxes that must end up showing matching colors. One idea is that the choice of color checked later helps determine what was inside earlier. That would be a backward-in-time influence. In quantum physics, some interpretations explore a similar possibility to explain how far-apart particles can have matching results without sending a usable message faster than light.
summaries.summary: Quantum theory is an extremely successful way to predict the results of experiments. However, it does not settle every question about what exists in the physical world. Retrocausal interpretations suggest that a future measurement setting may help determine an earlier state of a quantum system. This idea is not simply a claim that people can change ordinary history. In these interpretations, forward- and backward-in-time influences may work together to produce the correlations found in quantum experiments. Supporters think this could help avoid some problems involving distant connections, measurement settings, and the nature of the quantum state. The entry also explains that retrocausal ideas come in many forms, such as models using conditions at both an earlier and a later boundary. Critics worry about causal loops, hidden fine-tuning, and whether retrocausal models still have the kinds of contextual features that quantum theory seems to require. The topic remains an interpretation question rather than a settled description of reality.
key_ideas: Quantum theory predicts experiments very well, but scientists and philosophers still disagree about what reality is like underneath the predictions.
Some interpretations suggest that a later measurement choice might influence an earlier hidden state.
Retrocausality could offer a way to explain quantum connections while keeping influences connected through nearby points in space and time.
Time-symmetry, the idea that basic laws may work similarly forward and backward in time, is one reason some people consider retrocausality.
There are serious objections, including worries about confusing cause-and-effect loops and special arrangements that hide influences from ordinary signals.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic shows that science can make remarkably accurate predictions while leaving room for disagreement about what the predictions mean. It also introduces a big question about time: must causes always come before effects? Studying the debate helps us separate an experiment’s results from the different philosophical stories people use to explain those results.

important_terms.definition: A possible influence in which something that happens later helps bring about something earlier.
A theory used in physics to predict and explain what experiments will show.
A connection in which changing one thing can help change another thing.
The idea that influences should travel through nearby parts of space rather than jumping instantly across distance.
A quantum experiment result that depends partly on how the measurement is arranged.

questions_to_think_about: Would a later choice really change the past, or could it only be connected with the past?
Why might a physicist want an explanation that uses nearby influences instead of instant action at a distance?
If something is hidden and cannot be measured directly, how could we test a theory about it?
Can a theory be useful even when people disagree about what its unseen parts mean?

summaries.example: Consider an entanglement experiment with two distant measurement stations. The experimenters choose settings at each station and obtain correlated outcomes. Bell-type results show that theories satisfying Bell’s local-causality condition cannot reproduce all the quantum correlations. A retrocausal proposal instead allows a later setting to influence an earlier ontic state, while the influence remains connected through timelike routes. The proposal must still explain why these influences do not become ordinary controllable signals to the past.
summaries.summary: The entry surveys retrocausal approaches to the interpretation of quantum mechanics. Quantum theory accurately predicts experimental statistics, but the measurement problem leaves unsettled what physical reality underlies those statistics. Retrocausal interpretations permit later measurement choices to affect earlier ontic states. Their central motivation is that several quantum no-go theorems rely on an ontological-models framework containing measurement independence, an assumption that excludes such backward influence from the start. Dropping that assumption may allow models with more local, determinate, or psi-epistemic features, and may offer zigzag explanations of Bell correlations. A second motivation comes from time-symmetry: if fundamental laws and experimental descriptions are symmetric under time reversal, some arguments suggest that the underlying causal structure should be symmetric as well. The entry discusses models including the transactional interpretation, two-state-vector approaches, causally symmetric Bohmian models, two-time boundary models, and all-at-once Lagrangian proposals. It also presents objections. The bilking argument challenges the coherence of backward causation, while other critics identify retrocausality with superdeterminism or argue that it requires fine-tuning to avoid signaling. Finally, a generalized contextuality result suggests that allowing an exotic causal structure does not automatically recover noncontextuality. Thus retrocausality is presented as a serious but disputed strategy for interpreting quantum theory, not as an established physical conclusion.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes quantum theory’s predictive success from agreement about its underlying ontology, or account of what exists.
Retrocausal models challenge the measurement-independence assumption used in several no-go results, potentially reopening local hidden-variable or psi-epistemic approaches.
A retrocausal account need not mean faster-than-light action: a zigzag influence can connect distant events through earlier and later timelike segments, though its interpretation remains contested.
Arguments from time-symmetry claim that, under additional assumptions about quantum ontology or mediation, operational time-symmetry may require retrocausal influence.
The transactional interpretation uses forward- and backward-evolving waves, while other proposals use two boundary conditions, time-symmetric particle dynamics, or constrained fields.

Objections include bilking and causal-loop worries, the possibility that retrocausality is merely superdeterminism, fine-tuning needed to preserve no-signaling, and a theorem suggesting exotic causal structures remain contextual.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate links physics with questions about causation, time, explanation, and scientific realism. It shows how a theorem’s conclusion can depend on background assumptions about hidden states and experimental choices. It also demonstrates that solving one problem—such as Bell nonlocality—may create another, such as fine-tuning or contextuality. Understanding these trade-offs is important for evaluating interpretations rather than treating quantum mechanics as if its formal predictions had only one philosophical meaning.

important_terms.definition: The claim that a later event can causally influence an earlier event, usually understood through an intervention-based account of causation.
A description of causation in which changing one variable is an effective way to change another, without deciding in advance whether the relation is objectively real.
Bell’s condition that, once a suitable common past is specified, events in spacelike separated regions have no further causal dependence.
The assumption that an earlier hidden state is statistically independent of a later choice of measurement setting.
A theory in which operationally equivalent procedures have equivalent underlying representations; quantum results challenge such models.
An account treating the quantum state as representing incomplete information about a deeper physical state rather than as itself part of reality.
The principle that each statistical independence in a causal model reflects a causal independence, rather than a precisely balanced cancellation.
The idea that the basic laws or description of a system remain unchanged under an appropriate reversal of time.

questions_to_think_about: Does violating measurement independence by retrocausal influence differ fundamentally from violating it through superdeterminism?
Can causal language be appropriate in fundamental physics if the laws are represented by equations specifying a whole history?
Why might no-signaling statistical patterns create a fine-tuning problem for a theory that nevertheless contains causal links?
Would a time-symmetric theory naturally require backward causation, or could it represent time symmetrically without it?
If retrocausal models remain contextual, do they still achieve the classical ontology that motivates them?

summaries.example: Suppose two students each receive a card from a strange machine. Their cards often match even when the students are far apart. One explanation says the cards were coordinated by something in their shared past. Another says that the way the students later check their cards helps determine an earlier hidden arrangement. If the second explanation is used for a quantum experiment, it must explain the matching results without letting the students send an ordinary message into the past.
summaries.summary: Retrocausality in quantum mechanics is the proposal that events later in time can help cause or constrain events earlier in time. The idea appears in some interpretations of quantum theory because the theory predicts experimental correlations so successfully while leaving disagreement about the underlying reality. In particular, Bell-type and other no-go results rule out certain combinations of assumptions, such as local hidden variables with measurement independence. Retrocausal approaches challenge measurement independence: an earlier hidden state may depend on a later choice of measurement setting. Supporters hope this could explain distant quantum correlations through a zigzag pattern of nearby influences and might make room for a more classical or psi-epistemic picture of the quantum state. Time-symmetry is another motivation. If fundamental laws treat time directions alike, perhaps causal dependence should not be restricted to the future. The entry describes several proposals, including the transactional interpretation and models using both initial and final conditions. It also presents objections. Some philosophers argue that backward causation is incoherent or leads to causal loops. Others say the proposal is really superdeterminism, or that it requires carefully balanced influences to prevent signaling. A broader result suggests that retrocausal models may still face contextuality. The entry therefore presents an ongoing philosophical dispute, not a settled answer.
key_ideas: Quantum theory gives highly successful predictions, but its success does not settle what the quantum world is really like.
Retrocausal interpretations allow future measurement choices to play a causal role in earlier hidden conditions.
Supporters argue that dropping measurement independence may avoid some no-go results and provide a more local explanation of quantum correlations.
Time-symmetry gives another reason to consider backward influence, although time-symmetric laws do not automatically settle the issue.
Different models describe retrocausality in different ways, including two-time descriptions and exchanges of forward- and backward-evolving waves.
Critics raise concerns about causal loops, superdeterminism, fine-tuning, and contextuality.
summaries.why_it_matters: This subject helps explain why interpreting science involves more than checking predictions. Two theories can agree about what experiments will show while disagreeing about hidden states, causation, and the direction of time. Retrocausality also gives a clear example of how changing one assumption in an argument can reopen possibilities while producing new problems that must be addressed.

important_terms.definition: A proposed causal influence that runs from a later event toward an earlier event.
A connection in which an action or change helps produce a result.
The view that events separated by great distances should not directly influence one another outside the limits set by physics.
The choice of how an experiment is performed, such as which setting is selected for a measurement.
The assumption that an earlier hidden condition is not affected by a later measurement choice.
The idea that a result can depend on the larger arrangement or method used to measure it.
The view that the quantum state may represent an observer’s information rather than a complete physical object in the world.
The idea that the basic laws do not favor one direction of time over the other.

questions_to_think_about: If a future measurement affects an earlier hidden state, why might we still be unable to use it to change the past at will?
Is an explanation more satisfying if it keeps influences nearby, even if it requires unusual ideas about time?
What is the difference between a measurement revealing a value and helping bring that value about?
Could a theory be time-symmetric in its laws but not retrocausal in its interpretation?
Why might preserving no-signaling be a challenge for a theory that includes backward influences?
